directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Roseum Elegans is one of the most cold-hardy and widely adaptable rhododendron cultivars, tolerating heat, cold, and poor soil better than many fussier hybrids. Large, dense trusses of lavender-pink flowers with a faint orange-brown blotch cover this old, extremely reliable catawba rhododendron hybrid each late spring, backed by large, leathery, deep green evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure to a shaded border. Introduced in the nineteenth century and still one of the most widely planted rhododendron cultivars in North America, it owes its enduring popularity to exceptional cold hardiness, heat tolerance, and general toughness compared to more temperamental modern hybrids, thriving in a wider range of climates and soils. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid planting too deep or in poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nova Zembla is one of the most cold-hardy red-flowered rhododendron cultivars available, reliable in harsh winter climates.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nova Zembla is one of the most cold-hardy red-flowered rhododendron cultivars available, reliable in harsh winter climates. Bold trusses of vivid, true-red flowers with a subtle darker blotch open in late spring above large, dark evergreen leaves on a dense, rounded shrub, a classic old Dutch hybrid still widely grown for its dependable, exceptionally cold-hardy performance where less hardy red rhododendrons fail. Named for a remote Russian Arctic archipelago as an allusion to its extreme cold tolerance, it remains one of the standard red rhododendron choices for northern gardens, valued for its combination of hardiness and bold flower color. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells since shallow-rooted rhododendrons are sensitive to drought, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; PJM rhododendron is exceptionally cold-hardy and tolerates more sun than most large-leaved rhododendrons.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; PJM rhododendron is exceptionally cold-hardy and tolerates more sun than most large-leaved rhododendrons. Small, aromatic, dark green leaves turn an attractive plum-purple in cold weather, providing year-round color, and the shrub is smothered in a profusion of small, vivid lavender-pink flowers in very early spring, often the first rhododendron to bloom in a northern garden. Named for breeder Peter J. Mezitt and bred specifically for extreme cold hardiness, it tolerates far colder winters than most large-leaved rhododendron hybrids and adapts to more sun exposure, making it one of the most widely planted and reliable rhododendrons across the colder regions of North America. Mulch to keep roots cool, avoid planting in heavy or poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; English Roseum is a tough, adaptable, cold-hardy rhododendron widely used in commercial and municipal landscaping. Full, rounded trusses of clear pink flowers open in late spring above large, glossy, dark evergreen leaves on a dense, vigorous, well-branched shrub valued for its exceptional toughness and adaptability across a wide range of climates and soil conditions. One of the most commonly planted landscape rhododendrons in North America due to its reliability, heat and cold tolerance, and resistance to common rhododendron problems, it is a dependable choice for foundation plantings, mass plantings, and shaded borders where a fussier hybrid might struggle. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Percy Wiseman is a compact yakushimanum-type hybrid well suited to smaller gardens than many larger rhododendron cultivars. Flowers open a soft peachy-cream fading to pale primrose-yellow with a hint of pink at the edges, a subtle, changeable color combination typical of the finest yakushimanum-heritage hybrids, on a compact, dense, mounding shrub with attractive, felted new growth. Its manageable mature size, exceptional flower quality, and the sturdy constitution inherited from its Rhododendron yakushimanum parentage have made it a multi-award-winning cultivar and a favorite for smaller gardens where full-sized rhododendrons would be too large. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid hot afternoon sun in warmer zones, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostbo Red is one of the deepest red-budded mountain laurel cultivars and needs the same acidic, well-drained conditions as other mountain laurels.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostbo Red is one of the deepest red-budded mountain laurel cultivars and needs the same acidic, well-drained conditions as other mountain laurels. Deep, rich red buds open to reveal cupped, saucer-shaped flowers with a paler pink interior, opening in intricate, crimped, origami-like folds typical of mountain laurel, one of the earliest and darkest-red cultivars bred by pioneering Pacific Northwest hybridizer Endre Ostbo in the mid-twentieth century. Native to the eastern United States, mountain laurel is an important broadleaf evergreen understory shrub, and this early red-flowered selection helped spark the modern wave of mountain laurel breeding for improved bud and flower color that followed in subsequent decades. Provide the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and dappled shade the species requires, mulch to keep roots cool, and avoid heavy pruning, since mountain laurel resents hard cutting back.
